title: I saw All of Us Strangers and I need help mending my broken heart

commenti.body:
You should watch some of the Q&As on YouTube that Andrew Haigh has done.


Essentially, it doesn't matter what is real or not, because the main thing is that Adam is finally confronting his past trauma that has had him stuck for 30+ years. Whether he's doing that with ghosts, his imagination, his screenplay, he's the one finally making the decision to try to move forward.


This is best encapsulated by the exchange with his mom while he's in the K-Hole. He asks:


Is this real?


Does it feel real?


Yes.


Well then, there you go.


Now, after reading the synopsis of the book, seeing the Japanese version (which treats the situation much more matter-of-factly) and watching the movie a 3rd time, I came to the conclusion that his parents are ghosts. Whether they're on another plane, only in his head, whatever you believe a ghost to be, I think they're that. It makes his interactions with them much more meaningful, as well.


Even though it "doesn't matter," it's fun to dissect the reality of films like this (and I think that K-Hole in the middle of the movie is there to mess with the viewer's sense of time and reality), here is how I think it plays out.


Adam is trying to write a script about his childhood. He meets Harry when he shows up at Adam's door. I believe this is their only real interaction as living beings. Adam turns down Harry after Harry's line about "vampires at my door." What's even more tragic about this is that Adam had "The Power of Love" playing when Harry knocks on his door. One of the lines from that song is, "I'll protect you from the hooded claw, from the vampires at your door " Harry, sensing Adam isn't going to let him in, throws out a last ditch effort to win him over by quoting the song he was playing. Of course, Adam can't even connect the dots, too scared by the very drunk man confronting him head on. Understandably, it's a very creepy line for a drunk stranger trying to get into your apartment to say if you don't make the connection.


From there, I think Harry dies that night. In the last scene, Harry is wearing the same pink sweatshirt, his hand purple and the apartment stinking from decomposition, with the same bottle from that first night. They both even reference "that night" and how Harry was so scared and didn't want to be alone. Their conversation doesn't read to me like a couple that have had a super intense relationship.


The only thing I haven't quite settled on is whether the Harry that Adam starts having a relationship with is in his head or perhaps a ghost in denial of his own death. While the final scene plays more like he was a ghost, it's hard to deny that he is pretty much manic pixie dreamboy to Adam; exactly what he needs to pull him out of his hole.


Again, though, I'm not sure it even matters. Either way, Adam is now not only ready to accept love from others, he's ready to move on from love lost, as well, as we see him cuddling with Harry and essentially sending him off to the afterlife in the comfort of love.


All of Us Strangers was my favorite of 2023. One of the things that I think Haigh really nailed was, and I can't remember his exact words, but something to the effect of, "universality by specificity." Make something real enough to a single person and it can translate to all types of people. I'm not gay, I'm not British, my parents are still alive, and I suffered no childhood trauma, yet this movie connected with me on such a deep level.

This movie was so emotionally overwhelming. I cried like… 6 times throughout the movie. 

Regarding what’s real and what isn’t… I think this movie is more about the “feelings” it conveys rather than the “meaning”. It’s an emotional journey where a very broken, lonely man confronts the death of his parents, the lack of closure he had, and conflicted feelings about his sexuality. Tbh, for me the whole movie might have been just “a draft” of the piece Andrew Scott’s character was writing about his parents. It exists outside the real of what we consider “reality”. Only true cinema can achieve such a thing
